lead: A maximum entropy Markov model tags a sequence with a log-linear classifier at every position. Instead of one emission table, many overlapping features can fire: the word, its suffix, capitalisation, the previous tag, the next word. Each feature has a weight, and the weighted sum scores a candidate tag. The scores become local probabilities that sum to one at that position. Because the model is still a chain, Viterbi decodes the whole sentence. Taggers use it for part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition. Only a few universities teach this model, but it explains why CRFs exist. Some syllabi call it a conditional Markov model.
prereq: You need: 2.5 for the HMM chain and Viterbi, and the logistic regression and maximum entropy classifier from Unit 5.

sections.h3: Why the HMM emission table is too narrow

blocks.text: An HMM scores a tag sequence with two tables: transition P(ti | ti−1) and emission P(wi | ti). The emission sees one word only. It cannot ask whether the word ends in -ing, starts with a capital letter, contains a digit, or sits next to the word to. A tagger needs those clues together. For example, Chennai is a place because it is capitalised and appears after in; the single word identity may be unseen in training.

A maximum entropy Markov model (MEMM) replaces the emission table with a classifier at each position i. Let x = x<sub>1</sub> ... x<sub>n</sub> be the whole sentence, t<sub>i</sub> the tag at position i, and t<sub>i−1</sub> the previous tag. A feature function f<sub>j</sub>(i, t<sub>i−1</sub>, t<sub>i</sub>, x) returns 1 when its condition holds, else 0. Each feature has a weight λ<sub>j</sub>. The score of tag t<sub>i</sub> is the sum over all features that fire.
score(i, t<sub>i−1</sub>, t<sub>i</sub>, x) = Σ over j of λ<sub>j</sub> f<sub>j</sub>(i, t<sub>i−1</sub>, t<sub>i</sub>, x)
blocks.where: i is the position; t<sub>i</sub> is the candidate tag; t<sub>i−1</sub> is the previous tag; x is the whole sentence; f<sub>j</sub> is a feature function returning 0 or 1; λ<sub>j</sub> is a real-valued weight learned from data.

blocks.text: The local probability is a softmax over tags.
P(t<sub>i</sub> | t<sub>i−1</sub>, x) = exp(score(i, t<sub>i−1</sub>, t<sub>i</sub>, x)) ÷ Σ over t′ of exp(score(i, t<sub>i−1</sub>, t′, x))
blocks.where: exp(·) is the exponential function; t′ ranges over every possible tag at position i; the denominator normalises over tags at that position only, with the previous tag fixed.

blocks.text: Features can look anywhere in x. Typical ones are: current word equals flies; current word ends in ies; current word is capitalised; previous tag is N; next word is like; current word is in a small gazetteer of verbs. All fire for a candidate tag, so the classifier can combine spelling, context and tag history. The maximum entropy principle picks weights that make the model's feature counts on training data match the observed counts, while keeping the distribution as uniform as possible otherwise. We state that objective only; training uses iterative numerical methods.

The model is still a chain. The probability of a tag sequence t1 ... tn given x is P(t | x) = Π over i from 1 to n of P(ti | ti−1, x), with a fixed start tag t0. Π means multiply over positions i. Because each factor depends only on ti−1 and ti, Viterbi works exactly as in 2.5: keep the best score for each tag at each position, and backpointers recover the path. The only change is that the local score is a log-linear sum, not a table lookup.

sections.h3: Label bias and the HMM comparison

blocks.text: Per-position normalisation has a cost. Suppose a state offers only one outgoing tag. Its local probability is 1, so the model is barely penalised for taking that path, even when the observation is a poor match. A state with many outgoing choices spreads probability mass and is penalised. The path can therefore be chosen for its low branching rather than for the words. This is the label bias problem. It is the reason the next chapter, 2.7, normalises once over whole sequences.
Training maximises Σ log P(t<sub>i</sub> | t<sub>i−1</sub>, x) over training tokens and positions. The sum is over tagged tokens; the weights are shared across all positions.

examples.question: Token flies comes after tag N in the sentence being tagged. Two features fire for tag V: word = flies with weight 1.5, and previous tag = N with weight 0.2. For tag N: word = flies with weight 0.8, and previous tag = N with weight 0.5. No other features fire. Find the local probabilities P(N | N, flies) and P(V | N, flies).
steps: List the firing features for tag V. score(V) = 1.5 + 0.2 = 1.7.
List the firing features for tag N. score(N) = 0.8 + 0.5 = 1.3.
Exponentiate each score. exp(1.7) = 5.474 (3 decimal places) and exp(1.3) = 3.669 (3 decimal places).
Add to get the local normaliser. Z = 5.474 + 3.669 = 9.143.
Divide each exponential by Z. P(V | N, flies) = 5.474 ÷ 9.143 = 0.60 (2 decimal places). P(N | N, flies) = 3.669 ÷ 9.143 = 0.40 (2 decimal places).
examples.check:
import math
sV = 1.5 + 0.2
sN = 0.8 + 0.5
eV = math.exp(sV)
eN = math.exp(sN)
Z = eV + eN
pV = eV / Z
pN = eN / Z
print(round(sV, 1))
print(round(sN, 1))
print(round(eV, 3))
print(round(eN, 3))
print(round(Z, 3))
print(f'{pN:.2f}')
print(f'{pV:.2f}')

traps: The normaliser is per position over tags only. Dividing by a sum over all positions and histories gives a CRF, not a MEMM.
A MEMM is discriminative: it models P(t | x), not P(x, t). It is not an HMM with extra feature columns.
Label bias comes from per-state normalisation. Do not blame Viterbi or the feature set.
The previous tag is part of the feature vector, so the model is a first-order chain. If you drop t<sub>i−1</sub>, Viterbi no longer applies as a chain decoder.
Do not call one local probability a sentence probability. Multiply the local factors along a path to get the sequence probability.

quiz.q: What does a feature function f<sub>j</sub>(i, t<sub>i−1</sub>, t<sub>i</sub>, x) return in a MEMM?
quiz.a: It returns 0 or 1. It returns 1 when the feature condition holds for the candidate tag at position i, else 0.

quiz.q: Why can a MEMM use the suffix of a word while an HMM emission table cannot?
quiz.a: The HMM emission is a table indexed by the single word. The MEMM classifier can include a feature such as 'word ends in -ing' that fires for many words and combines with other features.

quiz.q: Two tags have scores 0.9 and 1.2 at one position; no other tags are possible. Find their local probabilities.
Explain label bias using a state that has only one outgoing transition.
quiz.a: That state's local probability is 1 whatever the observation, so it is not penalised. A state with several outgoing tags spreads mass and is penalised. The path can be chosen for low branching rather than for good word evidence.

quiz.q: Why does Viterbi still apply to a MEMM?
quiz.a: The sequence probability factorises into local factors P(t<sub>i</sub> | t<sub>i−1</sub>, x). Each factor depends only on the current and previous tag, so the model is a chain and Viterbi dynamic programming applies.

quiz.q: Give another name for a maximum entropy Markov model.
A student normalises the score at each position by the sum over all tags at all positions. What model does that resemble, and why is it not a MEMM?
quiz.a: Global normalisation over whole sequences is the CRF idea of 2.7. A MEMM normalises at each position over tags only, with the previous tag fixed.

beyond: Not for the exam. MEMMs were widely used in part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition and shallow parsing before CRFs. The label bias insight led to globally normalised models, then to structured perceptrons, and later to neural taggers such as BiLSTM-CRF and transformer token classifiers. Modern sequence labelling usually learns contextual embeddings and a CRF or span head, but the MEMM idea of many overlapping features at each position still appears in feature engineering and in the log-linear view of attention. Search next for 'maximum entropy Markov model', 'label bias problem' and 'conditional random field'.
